draft.title: Autonomy and interdependence
card: The ability to make your own choices and act on them. Young people usually gain more autonomy as they grow, such as choosing subjects, friends or a part-time job.
People rely on each other and each gives something back. Family, friends, schools and communities all depend on one another in some way.
Gaining autonomy does not end interdependence. A young person can make more of their own choices and still rely on others for money, advice, care or a place to live.
How much autonomy a young person has, and when, can differ between families and cultures. Many families expect young people to keep close ties and share responsibilities.
draft.remember: Growing up usually brings more autonomy, but people still depend on others.

a.q: Which example shows a young person using autonomy?
opts: Priya chooses which subjects to study in Year 11
Priya's parents drive her to school each morning
Priya's cousin helps her with a maths task
Priya's family hosts a dinner each Sunday night
a.why: Autonomy is making your own choices, and Priya choosing her own subjects is that. The lift to school is a case of relying on others, so it shows dependence, not a choice she makes.
a.clue: Look for the option where the young person is the one deciding.

b.q: Tom, 17, rents a room, pays for his own phone and picks his own friends. He still asks his uncle for advice on big decisions. What does this show?
opts: Autonomy and interdependence exist together
Tom has lost his autonomy by asking for advice
Tom is fully independent of other people
Tom has not gained any autonomy yet
b.why: Tom makes many of his own choices, which is autonomy, and still relies on his uncle's advice, which is interdependence. Asking for advice does not remove his autonomy, so the idea that he has lost it is wrong.
b.clue: Can a person make their own choices and still rely on others?

a.best: Priya chooses which subjects to study in Year 11
